newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy needs more budget steps for EMU - researchers.
newsitem.headline: Italy needs more budget steps for EMU - researchers.

text.p: The Italian government's 1997 budget for Europe will not be enough to reduce the deficit/GDP ratio to three percent next year, Italian private research body IRS said in a report.
And the goal, an essential Maastricht objective for entry into the single European currency, will not even be met in 1998 without extra measures, IRS said.
IRS, in its latest economic report, said Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government was "counting too much on a European recovery, on a rise in household consumption and on an upturn in investments."
Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco said earlier on Tuesday Italy might not have to present any corrective measures in 1997.
If it does, they will only be of limited scope, he told the lower house of parliament's budget committee.
The budget is designed to slice 62.5 trillion lire off next year's deficit -- double the size in the originally planned package.
"This will limit to the full, if not render superfluous, a mini-budget for next year," Visco said.
But IRS said in its report the government "is cheating a bit to inspire confidence, but its game is too obvious."
It said some figures in the budget were "ambiguous" and the effect of some savings measures had been over-estimated.

IRS said if in the second half of 1997 average interest rates on Treasury debt issues were near 5.5 percent, then the deficit/GDP ratio, based on the European Union's definition, would be 4.2 percent.
In 1998, even with a half-point fall in rates, the ratio would still be above the three-percent level, at 3.3 percent.
To get the ratio down below 3.0 percent, a new corrective measure would be needed "more or less equal to the budget for Europe proposed for 1997," IRS said.
